title: The First Crusade march to Jerusalem
summary: Responding to Pope Urban II's call, crusader armies left western Europe in 1096 and gathered at Constantinople. They took Nicaea and won at Dorylaeum in 1097, captured Antioch in June 1098, and took Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, after which many of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants were killed.

uncertainty.note: Pages differ on small points: World History Encyclopedia sets the departure at 15 August 1096 while its timeline lists March 1096 for Peter the Hermit's army; the Historical Association says the first armies left in April and May 1096 despite the announced 15 August; Nicaea surrendered on 19 June 1097 (Historical Association) and June 1097 (World History Encyclopedia). The year of arrival at Constantinople is autumn-winter 1096 in the article text and 1097 in its timeline.

as_recorded.value: The departure date was set for 15 August

importance.justification: The expedition that took Jerusalem in 1099 and led to the founding of the crusader states, a landmark of medieval Europe-Middle East relations.

audience_note: Describes military conquest and the mass killing of Muslim and Jewish inhabitants of Jerusalem in 1099, and notes attacks on Jewish communities by crusader groups in the Rhineland.

beats.caption: Crusader armies leave western Europe in 1096, the first groups before the announced August date, and gather at Constantinople.
In 1097 the crusaders take Nicaea, which surrenders to the Byzantines, and defeat the Seljuk Turks at Dorylaeum.
After taking Antioch in 1098, the army storms Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 and a mass killing of Muslims and Jews follows.

reviewer_note: Least sure: arrival year at Constantinople (1096 vs 1097 on the same page) and the exact date of the Nicaea surrender. The route is the main line only; Edessa and Cilicia detachments are not plotted. Dorylaeum is plotted at the ancient city's Wikidata point; Edgington says the exact battle site is unknown. The Jerusalem death toll is disputed on the page and is not given here.
